blocks.text: SLE is an uncommon multisystem autoimmune disease. About **90% of patients are women**, typically first presenting at **20–30 years** (Kumar gives 20–40). Prevalence is around 0.03% in Caucasians but roughly 0.2% in Afro-Caribbeans, and African Americans are affected 2–4 times as often as white Americans.

Proposed mechanism: apoptotic cells are **cleared poorly**, so nuclear self-antigens (DNA, histones) reach the immune system. This drives polyclonal **B- and T-cell activation**, autoantibody production and **immune-complex deposition with complement activation**, causing vasculitis and organ damage. Genetic risk includes HLA variants (HLA-DR2/DR3) and rare **homozygous C1q, C2 or C4 deficiency**, which carries a high risk. **UV light and infection** trigger flares.

blocks.title: Organ involvement in SLE
rows: Arthralgia in ~90%, with morning stiffness; tenosynovitis
Swollen synovitis is rare. Deformity (Jaccoud's) comes from tendon damage. **No erosions**
Malar rash (up to 20%), discoid rash, photosensitivity, diffuse alopecia, urticaria, livedo reticularis
Malar rash **spares the nasolabial folds**. Discoid lesions scar; photosensitivity goes with anti-Ro
Raynaud's phenomenon, often years before other features
Secondary Raynaud's clues: onset >25 y, no family history, male
Pleurisy and exudative (often bilateral) effusions are commonest; pneumonitis, atelectasis
'Shrinking lung': restrictive defect with raised hemidiaphragms
Premature atherosclerosis: stroke and MI risk greatly increased
Proliferative GN with haematuria, proteinuria and casts
A main determinant of prognosis: monitor urinalysis and BP
Fatigue, headache, poor concentration; psychosis, seizures, chorea, visual hallucinations, transverse myelitis, lymphocytic meningitis
Non-specific symptoms often occur without lab evidence of activity
Mouth ulcers (may be painless), peritoneal serositis, mesenteric vasculitis
Mesenteric vasculitis can infarct or perforate bowel
Retinal vasculitis (infarcts seen as hard exudates), episcleritis, optic neuritis

blocks.title: Course and general features
items: Fever, weight loss and mild lymphadenopathy appear during **flares**. Fatigue and low-grade joint pain can persist regardless of activity.
The course **relapses and remits**. Rash, joint pain and fatigue are the usual first features; kidney, lung, heart and nervous system involvement come with more advanced disease.
Juvenile-onset SLE has more renal, skin and neuropsychiatric disease than adult-onset disease.
Pregnancy problems include recurrent miscarriage, growth restriction, pre-eclampsia and preterm labour.

blocks.text: Primary Raynaud's is common (up to 5% of people). Suspect a **secondary** cause such as SLE when onset is after 25, there is no family history, or the patient is male. Nail-fold capillary dropout with dilated, branching loops points more towards systemic sclerosis (or severe primary Raynaud's).
New hip or knee pain in a patient with SLE: think **avascular necrosis**, a rare complication of the disease itself or of corticosteroid therapy.
Suspected cerebral lupus: **exclude infection**, or treat it in parallel, before giving high-dose steroids and immunosuppression.

Sources disagree on **Libman–Sacks endocarditis**. Davidson lists it as a recognised feature (sterile fibrin vegetations linked to antiphospholipid antibodies); Kumar calls it very rare. Kumar and Zero to Finals describe it as non-infective and mainly mitral, and Zero to Finals links it to both SLE and APS.

blocks.note: Look at: **malar rash** across the cheeks that **spares the nasolabial folds**. Rosacea is the main mimic.
Look at: severe **secondary Raynaud's** with digital ulceration, a pointer to an autoimmune connective tissue disease.
Compare **chronic discoid lupus** (scaly plaques healing with atrophy and depigmentation) with the macular malar erythema of SLE.
Summary diagram of SLE features by organ system: a useful revision map.

blocks.text: Diagnosis rests on a combination of clinical features and laboratory results. Criteria sets were built to **classify** patients for research, not to diagnose individuals, but exams expect you to know them. Davidson uses the classic **11-item system**: an adult is classified as having SLE when **any 4 of 11** features are present, at the same time or one after another.

blocks.title: The 11 classification criteria (Davidson Box 24.63)
rows: Fixed flat or raised erythema sparing the nasolabial folds
Raised red patches with adherent keratotic scale and follicular plugging
Rash from an abnormal reaction to sunlight
Oral or nasopharyngeal ulcers, which may be painless
Non-erosive, in **2 or more peripheral joints**
Persistent proteinuria **> 0.5 g/24 h** or cellular casts
Seizures or psychosis with no drug or metabolic cause
Haemolytic anaemia, WCC < 4, lymphocytes < 1 or platelets < 100 (× 10⁹/L); counts on **two occasions**
Anti-DNA at abnormal titre, anti-Sm, or antiphospholipid antibodies

blocks.title: 2012 SLICC criteria
items: Classify as SLE with **≥ 4 criteria including ≥ 1 clinical and ≥ 1 immunological**, OR with **biopsy-proven lupus nephritis plus a positive ANA or anti-dsDNA**.

Clinical: acute or chronic cutaneous lupus, oral/nasal ulcers, non-scarring alopecia, synovitis of ≥ 2 joints, serositis, renal (500 mg protein/24 h or red cell casts), neurological, haemolytic anaemia, leucopenia/lymphopenia, thrombocytopenia.
Immunological: ANA, anti-dsDNA, anti-Sm, antiphospholipid antibodies, **low complement** (C3, C4, CH50), and a **positive Coombs test without haemolysis**.

blocks.title: 2019 EULAR/ACR classification
items: **Entry criterion:** ANA titre **≥ 1:80**. Then **≥ 10 points**, with at least one clinical criterion.
Only the **highest-weighted item in each domain** is counted.
Top weights: class III/IV nephritis **10**; class II/V nephritis 8; anti-dsDNA or anti-Sm 6; acute cutaneous lupus 6; joint involvement 6; acute pericarditis 6.
Lower weights: seizure 5; pleural/pericardial effusion 5; proteinuria > 0.5 g/day 4; low C3 **and** C4 4; fever 2.

blocks.text: Common threads across all criteria sets: proteinuria **> 0.5 g/day**, arthritis in **≥ 2 joints**, and the SLE-specific antibodies **anti-dsDNA and anti-Sm**. Renal biopsy evidence of lupus nephritis carries the most weight in both SLICC and EULAR/ACR.
In real-world use the 2019 EULAR/ACR criteria may be **less sensitive** than the older ACR or 2012 SLICC sets, and all of them are classification tools. A patient can have SLE without meeting them.

sections.title: Laboratory tests for diagnosis and monitoring

blocks.title: Autoantibodies in SLE
rows: Screening test. **Negative ANA virtually excludes SLE**. Titre does **not** reflect activity
Very high titres: renal or CNS disease. **Rising titre may precede relapse**. Crithidia assay is highly specific; ELISA is not
Photosensitivity, subacute cutaneous lupus, thrombocytopenia; maternal anti-Ro causes **neonatal lupus and congenital heart block**
Mixed connective tissue disease; Raynaud's; nephritis less likely

blocks.title: Other results typical of active SLE
items: **Raised ESR**, with leucopenia, **lymphopenia**, anaemia (chronic disease or haemolytic) and thrombocytopenia. The degree of lymphopenia is a good activity marker.
**CRP is often normal** unless there is serositis.
**Low C3** from complement consumption by immune complexes. Low C4 is less specific.
Urea and creatinine rise **late** in nephritis. Low albumin or a raised urine albumin:creatinine ratio are earlier clues.
Raised immunoglobulins reflect B-cell activation.

blocks.title: Baseline workup
items: ANA first; if positive, anti-dsDNA, anti-Sm, anti-Ro, anti-La and anti-RNP.
FBC, antiphospholipid antibodies, C3 and C4.
Electrolytes, creatinine, urinalysis with sediment, and quantified urine protein.
Renal biopsy if GFR falls, the sediment is active, or there is significant proteinuria.

blocks.title: Which tests track activity?
rows: Anti-Sm, anti-Ro (diagnostic or association markers only)
CRP (normal in most flares; a high CRP suggests infection)

blocks.text: The trio of **high ESR, high anti-dsDNA and low C3** may herald a flare, and these normalise as it settles. In some patients anti-dsDNA stays high even in clinical remission.
A patient with SLE who has a **high CRP** should be assumed to have **infection** until proven otherwise, unless there is clear serositis.

A positive ANA alone does not mean lupus. It occurs in systemic sclerosis, Sjögren's, myositis, MCTD, autoimmune hepatitis, RA, drug-induced lupus and, at low titre, in healthy people, especially the elderly.

Reported ANA sensitivity varies: Davidson gives ~100%, Pocket Medicine 95–99% in active disease, Zero to Finals about 85%. Some authorities accept **ANA-negative lupus** (often anti-Ro positive). For the exam, follow Davidson: a negative ANA makes SLE very unlikely.
Persistently low C3 and C4 may reflect an **inherited C1, C2 or C4 deficiency** rather than consumption. Testing family members helps separate the two.

blocks.note: Diagnostic algorithm: clinical suspicion, then ANA, then specific antibodies.

blocks.text: Overt renal disease affects at least **one-third** of patients (Pocket Medicine says ~40%), and a quarter of these reach end-stage kidney disease within 10 years. The commonest presentation is **subacute**: haematuria, hypertension, variable renal impairment and heavy, often **nephrotic-range proteinuria**. It can also present as florid rapidly progressive GN or pure nephrotic syndrome.

blocks.title: ISN/RPS classes of lupus nephritis
rows: Mesangial immune deposits; normal light microscopy
None specific; HCQ ± steroids or ACE inhibitor
Focal proliferative lesions (only part of the glomeruli involved)
Induction: steroids + MMF or IV cyclophosphamide
Nephrotic syndrome, hypertension, renal insufficiency. **Commonest and most severe**
As class III; then MMF (or azathioprine) maintenance
Membranous pattern; may coexist with III/IV
ACE inhibitor; MMF + steroids if nephrotic range

blocks.title: Immunopathology and other renal lesions
items: Immunofluorescence shows IgG, IgM, IgA, C3, C4 and C1q: the **‘full house’** pattern.
Linked with anti-dsDNA and anti-Ro antibodies, and low serum C3, C4 and especially **C1q**.
Extraglomerular lesions: tubulointerstitial nephritis (75%), renal vein thrombosis, renal artery stenosis.
**Thrombotic microangiopathy** in the kidney points to antiphospholipid antibodies.

blocks.title: Detecting and assessing nephritis
items: Check **urinalysis and blood pressure regularly** in every patient.
Quantify proteinuria (urine protein:creatinine ratio) and look for red cell casts.
For a nephritic presentation, the serology screen includes ANA, dsDNA, C3 and C4.
**Renal biopsy** defines the class and guides treatment, and is often repeated to judge response.

blocks.text: Management: high-dose glucocorticoids with **IV cyclophosphamide** reduce progression to ESKD. Steroids with **mycophenolate mofetil** work as well for induction and maintenance. MMF is the preferred maintenance agent (superior to azathioprine), and all classes benefit from hydroxychloroquine. Treat hypertension and oedema in every case.
In about 25% of patients the class changes between serial biopsies. Classes I, II and V carry the best prognosis; class VI usually predicts ESKD.

Cyclophosphamide vs MMF: Davidson says MMF with steroids gives renal results **similar** to pulsed cyclophosphamide with fewer adverse effects. Kumar adds that cyclophosphamide may be **inferior in Black and Hispanic patients**. MMF is favoured in young patients who want to preserve fertility.

blocks.note: Histology of **class IV diffuse proliferative** lupus nephritis: endothelial and mesangial cell proliferation.

blocks.text: Goals: educate the patient, control symptoms, prevent organ damage and keep function. Everyone needs **sun avoidance and high-factor sunscreen** (Davidson SPF 25–50; Washington SPF ≥ 30 for all patients, not only those with photosensitive rashes), **smoking cessation** and control of cardiovascular risk factors.

blocks.title: Treatment by severity (Davidson)
rows: Analgesics, NSAIDs, **hydroxychloroquine**; topical steroids for skin
Prednisolone 5–20 mg/day plus a steroid-sparing agent: methotrexate, azathioprine or MMF. Higher steroid doses for flares, pleurisy or pericarditis
Pulsed IV methylprednisolone (10 mg/kg) + IV cyclophosphamide (15 mg/kg) every 2–3 weeks for 6 cycles; or high-dose steroids + MMF
Prednisolone 40–60 mg/day tapered to ≤ 10–15 mg/day by 3 months, plus azathioprine, methotrexate or MMF at the lowest effective dose

blocks.title: Other management points
items: **Hydroxychloroquine for every patient with active disease**, continued after remission because it reduces flares. It needs baseline and periodic eye checks.
Life-threatening disease (RPGN, active CNS lupus, severe thrombocytopenia) can be treated with IV methylprednisolone 500–1000 mg daily for 3–5 days.
Methotrexate is used mainly for joint and skin disease.
Newer agents: belimumab (also added at nephritis induction), voclosporin added to MMF + steroids for nephritis, and anifrolumab (anti-interferon receptor) for moderate–severe disease.
Before immunosuppression, give influenza and pneumococcal vaccines. **Avoid live vaccines** once immunosuppressed, and consider *Pneumocystis* prophylaxis with cyclophosphamide.
Screen for **osteoporosis and vitamin D deficiency** (biochemistry and DXA). Patients with SLE, APS and previous thrombosis need **life-long warfarin**.

blocks.text: Pregnancy: fertility is usually normal. Disease that is active at conception flares more, and flares are common **postpartum**. **Stop mycophenolate**; azathioprine, hydroxychloroquine and low-dose prednisolone are safe. Telling a flare from **pre-eclampsia** can be difficult. Anti-Ro/La-positive mothers risk **neonatal lupus** (rash, hepatitis, congenital heart block).

Exam pattern: **HCQ for all**, steroids for flares, a steroid-sparing agent to cut steroid exposure, and **cyclophosphamide or MMF** with high-dose steroids only for organ-threatening (renal/CNS/cardiac) disease.

Rituximab is **not** a standard SLE drug. Davidson notes that randomised trials did not show overall efficacy and it is used off-label in selected cases. Kumar suggests a possible role in severe refractory nephritis.

SLE follows an **episodic course** of flares and remissions, though some patients have chronic persistent disease. Ten-year survival is about **90%**, lower with major organ involvement. Davidson cites a **fivefold** increase in mortality versus age- and sex-matched controls, mainly from **premature cardiovascular disease**.

blocks.title: Causes of death over time
rows: Thrombosis (especially with antiphospholipid antibodies); raised risk of cancers, especially **lymphoma**

blocks.title: Prognostic factors
items: Renal involvement is one of the main determinants of outcome. Nephritis remits in fewer than half, and over 10% progress to ESKD.
Men have more severe disease than women. Disease is milder in older patients and more severe in children.
Higher mortality is reported in Black patients.
Coronary and peripheral vascular disease is accelerated by high disease activity and long-term steroids.

blocks.text: Good renal prognosis: classes I, II and V, and normalisation of proteinuria, blood pressure and renal function on treatment. Class VI usually means ESKD. Once renal failure develops, lupus activity often **settles**, and dialysis and transplantation work well.

Mortality figures differ: Davidson gives a **fivefold** increase, Pocket Medicine 2–3 times the general population. Use Davidson's figure, and remember that **cardiovascular disease** is the leading late cause.

Antiphospholipid syndrome (APS) is **thrombosis and/or pregnancy morbidity** with **persistent** antiphospholipid antibodies. It is primary when it occurs alone and **secondary** when it occurs with another disease, most often **SLE**. Other associations include RA, systemic sclerosis, Behçet's, temporal arteritis and Sjögren's. Antiphospholipid antibodies are found in 25–40% of people with SLE, but not all of them develop APS.

blocks.title: Laboratory tests
rows: Prolongs phospholipid-dependent clotting tests (APTT, dRVVT). Does **not correct with mixing**; corrects with excess phospholipid. PT unaffected
Moderate–high titre IgG/IgM. Causes a **false-positive VDRL/RPR**
Antibody to the main phospholipid-binding protein
Positive on **≥ 2 occasions ≥ 12 weeks apart**. ‘Triple-positive’ patients carry the highest thrombotic risk

blocks.title: Clinical features
items: **Arterial or venous** thrombosis, unlike most thrombophilias: DVT in ~40%, ischaemic stroke in ~20%.
Pregnancy: **≥ 3 recurrent first-trimester miscarriages**, unexplained death of a normal fetus after 10 weeks, or severe early pre-eclampsia.
Thrombocytopenia, Coombs-positive haemolysis, valve disease, **livedo reticularis**, skin necrosis, chorea, transverse myelitis.
**Catastrophic APS**: infarction of **≥ 3 organ systems within a week** with tissue microthrombi. Mortality is high (~44%); treat with plasmapheresis and rituximab.

blocks.title: Management
rows: Heparin then **long-term warfarin**. Pocket/ZtF target INR 2–3; arterial events may add aspirin. Kumar: lower INR target for venous than arterial events
Higher INR (3–4) or switch to LMWH/fondaparinux
**LMWH + low-dose aspirin** from early gestation; warfarin is contraindicated
Rivaroxaban is inferior to warfarin in triple-positive patients

blocks.text: The name **lupus anticoagulant** misleads: it prolongs clotting in the test tube but is **prothrombotic** in the body, and it is not a test for lupus.

INR targets vary between sources. Step-Up gives 2.5–3.5 for all patients, while Pocket Medicine uses **2–3** for a first event (INR 3–4 or LMWH if thrombosis recurs on warfarin) and Zero to Finals also gives 2–3. Davidson recommends warfarin rather than aspirin after APS-related arterial thrombosis.
In SLE patients with antiphospholipid antibodies, **hydroxychloroquine lowers the risk of thrombosis**: another reason to give HCQ to everyone.

blocks.note: Look at: **livedo reticularis**, a net-like violaceous mottling seen in SLE and antiphospholipid syndrome.

blocks.title: Classic culprit drugs
items: High-yield: **procainamide, hydralazine, isoniazid, chlorpromazine** (Davidson Box 24.78).
Also: methyldopa, quinidine, minocycline, penicillamine, diltiazem, interferons and **anti-TNF agents** (especially infliximab).
Skin-predominant drug lupus (Davidson dermatology) also lists ACE inhibitors, β-blockers, thiazides, anticonvulsants, lithium and PPIs.

blocks.title: Drug-induced vs idiopathic SLE
rows: ANA +, **anti-histone +**; anti-dsDNA and anti-Sm negative; **normal complement**
Anti-dsDNA/anti-Sm may be +; low C3/C4 when active
Usually resolves **4–6 weeks** after stopping the drug

blocks.text: Kidney or CNS involvement should make you think of **idiopathic SLE**, not drug-induced lupus.

Anti-histone sensitivity differs by source: Davidson ~80%, Pocket Medicine ~95%, and Step-Up gives >95% and states that it is always present. Follow Davidson: anti-histone is typical but a negative result does not completely exclude drug-induced lupus. **Anti-TNF** lupus is the exception, often with **positive anti-dsDNA** and sometimes negative anti-histone.
Management is simply to **stop the drug**. Most patients improve, so the prognosis is much better than idiopathic SLE.

sections.title: Drugs used in SLE: mechanisms and adverse effects

blocks.title: Conventional drugs
rows: Osteoporosis, diabetes, mood change (depression, mania, insomnia), neutrophilia, cataracts, myopathy, avascular necrosis, adrenal suppression
Unclear: blocks Toll-like receptors, impairs antigen presentation, raises lysosomal pH
**Retinal toxicity**, nightmares, skin pigmentation, myopathy, Stevens–Johnson
Converted to **6-mercaptopurine**; blocks DNA synthesis and lymphocyte proliferation
**Marrow suppression**, nausea, raised LFTs, lymphoproliferative disease
**TPMT** variants raise toxicity; safe in pregnancy
Inhibits **IMP dehydrogenase**, blocking guanosine synthesis in lymphocytes
**Alkylating agent**: cross-links DNA and halts cell division
Marrow suppression, nausea, alopecia, cardiotoxicity, **haemorrhagic cystitis**, bladder cancer, infertility, teratogenicity

blocks.title: Biologics
rows: Anti-**CD20**: complement-mediated lysis gives months of B-cell depletion
Infusion reactions, infections, hypogammaglobulinaemia, rarely **PML (JC virus)**. Off-label in SLE (ITP, AIHA, refractory disease)
Monoclonal antibody against **BAFF/BLyS**, the B-cell survival factor
Less immunosuppressive than rituximab. Used after poor response to steroids + HCQ

blocks.text: **Azathioprine + allopurinol**: allopurinol (a xanthine oxidase inhibitor) blocks breakdown of 6-MP, so marrow toxicity follows unless the azathioprine dose is cut by about **75%**.
**Cyclophosphamide**: prevent haemorrhagic cystitis with **mesna** (binds urotoxic metabolites) and good hydration. Offer sperm or oocyte storage because of azoospermia and premature menopause.
Hydroxychloroquine eye risk: retinal changes in up to **7.5%** on long-term treatment, more above **5 mg/kg/day**. Check vision before starting and at intervals (yearly per Step-Up).
Pregnancy-safe: **HCQ, azathioprine, low-dose prednisolone**. Must stop: **mycophenolate** (teratogenic). Cyclophosphamide is also teratogenic.
Steroids raise the white cell count (mainly neutrophils). Do not read neutrophilia in a steroid-treated SLE patient as proof of infection.

cards.front: Sex and age profile of SLE (Davidson)
cards.back: ~90% female; peak onset 20–30 years; commoner in Afro-Caribbeans

cards.front: Which part of the face does the malar rash of SLE spare?
cards.back: The **nasolabial folds**. Rosacea is a mimic

cards.front: Joint involvement in SLE: erosive or non-erosive?
cards.back: **Non-erosive**. Arthralgia in ~90%; deformity (Jaccoud's) comes from tendon damage

cards.front: Most common cardiac manifestation of SLE?
‘Shrinking lung syndrome’ in SLE?
cards.back: Restrictive defect with small lung volumes and **raised hemidiaphragms**

cards.front: How many of the 11 classic criteria classify a patient as SLE?
2019 EULAR/ACR entry criterion and threshold?
cards.back: ANA **≥ 1:80**, then **≥ 10 points** with ≥ 1 clinical criterion

cards.front: SLICC 2012: single finding that classifies with positive ANA/dsDNA?
ANA sensitivity and specificity for SLE (Davidson)?
cards.back: Sensitivity ~**100%**, specificity only **10–40%**: a negative ANA virtually excludes SLE

cards.front: Which antibody titre rises before an SLE relapse?
cards.back: **Anti-dsDNA**. Very high titres go with renal/CNS disease

cards.front: Maternal antibody causing congenital heart block?
SLE patient with a markedly raised CRP: think…?
cards.back: **Infection**. CRP is usually normal in a flare unless there is serositis

cards.front: Commonest and most severe class of lupus nephritis?
Lupus nephritis class that will not respond to immunosuppression?
Immunofluorescence pattern in lupus nephritis?
cards.back: **‘Full house’**: IgG, IgM, IgA, C3, C4 and C1q

cards.front: Drug every patient with active SLE should receive?
Which SLE drug must be stopped before pregnancy?
Main late cause of death in SLE?
Time between tests needed to confirm persistent antiphospholipid antibodies?
Anticoagulation for APS in pregnancy?
Four classic causes of drug-induced lupus (Davidson)?
Characteristic serology in drug-induced lupus?
Mechanism of mycophenolate mofetil?
cards.back: Inhibits **inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase**, blocking guanosine synthesis in lymphocytes

cards.front: Azathioprine dose change when allopurinol is started?
Target of rituximab, and a rare fatal complication?
cards.back: **CD20** on B cells; **PML** from JC virus

questions.leadIn: Match each patient below with the single best option from the list. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.
options: Avascular necrosis of the femoral head

items.stem: A 33-year-old woman has had SLE for 4 years and took prednisolone 30 mg daily for most of the last year. She now has right groin pain when walking, and internal rotation of the hip is painful and limited. The joint is not swollen.
items.explanation: Groin pain with restricted hip rotation in a patient on long-term steroids is **avascular necrosis**, a rare complication of SLE or its treatment.

items.stem: A 28-year-old woman with SLE has 6 months of increasing breathlessness. Chest X-ray shows small lung volumes, raised hemidiaphragms and clear lung fields. Lung function tests show a restrictive pattern with no evidence of fibrosis on CT.
items.explanation: Restriction with **raised hemidiaphragms** and normal lung parenchyma is **shrinking lung syndrome**.

items.stem: A 41-year-old woman with long-standing SLE has ulnar deviation of the fingers resembling rheumatoid hands. The joints are not swollen and hand X-rays show no erosions.
items.explanation: Two steps: an RA-like deformity with no erosions means it is not erosive synovitis, and in SLE such deformity comes from tendon damage. This is **Jaccoud's arthropathy**.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old woman is being assessed for SLE using the 11-criterion classification system. Her urine dipstick shows protein.
questions.leadIn: Which finding would satisfy the renal criterion?
options: Persistent proteinuria above 0.5 g per 24 hours
A single urine dipstick reading of 1+ protein
Serum creatinine above the upper limit of normal
Leucocyturia with a negative urine culture
questions.explanation: The renal criterion needs **persistent proteinuria > 0.5 g/24 h** or **cellular casts**. The same threshold appears in SLICC and EULAR/ACR.
whyNot: A single dipstick is not quantified or shown to be persistent.
Creatinine is not part of the renal criterion and rises late.
Haematuria alone does not count; cellular casts do.
Sterile pyuria is not a classification criterion.

questions.stem: A research team is classifying patients with the 2019 EULAR/ACR criteria. One patient has class IV lupus nephritis on biopsy, and a complete autoantibody panel has been sent.
questions.leadIn: Which result must be present before any points are counted?
options: ANA at a titre of at least 1:80
questions.explanation: EULAR/ACR 2019 uses **ANA ≥ 1:80 as an entry criterion**. Only then are weighted points added (≥ 10 needed). Class III/IV nephritis alone scores 10.
whyNot: Anti-dsDNA scores 6 points but is not the entry requirement.
Anti-Sm scores 6 points within the same domain as dsDNA; it is not required.
Low C3 and C4 scores 4 points, not entry.
Antiphospholipid antibodies score only 2 points.

questions.theme: Autoantibodies and laboratory tests in SLE
questions.leadIn: Match each patient below with the single best option from the list. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.

items.stem: A 30-year-old woman with a photosensitive rash is 22 weeks pregnant. A routine scan shows a fetal heart rate of 50/min with complete heart block.
items.explanation: Maternal **anti-Ro** crosses the placenta and causes **neonatal lupus and congenital heart block**. It is also linked with photosensitivity.

items.stem: A 24-year-old woman has tiredness and aching joints. Her GP wants one screening test which, if negative, would make SLE very unlikely.
items.explanation: **ANA** is ~100% sensitive but poorly specific, so a negative result virtually excludes SLE.

items.stem: A 35-year-old woman with SLE and previous nephritis is in remission. Her rheumatologist wants a serial antibody titre whose rise may give early warning of a renal relapse.
items.explanation: Rising **anti-dsDNA** titres may precede relapse, and very high titres go with renal and CNS disease. ANA titre does not track activity.

questions.leadIn: Match each patient below with the single best option from the list. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.
options: Class I minimal mesangial lupus nephritis
Class II mesangial proliferative lupus nephritis
Class IV diffuse proliferative lupus nephritis
Class VI advanced sclerosing lupus nephritis

items.stem: A 38-year-old woman has had SLE for 15 years. eGFR is 12 mL/min. Biopsy shows that 95% of glomeruli are globally sclerosed, with no active inflammation.
items.explanation: **Class VI**: ≥ 90% global sclerosis with no activity. Immunosuppression will not help; plan renal replacement.

items.stem: A 26-year-old woman with SLE has new hypertension, rising creatinine and heavy proteinuria with red cell casts. Biopsy shows diffuse endothelial and mesangial proliferation with subendothelial deposits.
items.explanation: **Diffuse** proliferation with **subendothelial deposits** is **class IV**, the commonest and most severe class.

items.stem: A 32-year-old woman with SLE has ankle oedema and 6 g/day of proteinuria. Her urine sediment is bland and BP is normal. The biopsy shows no proliferation, and she is told this class carries a relatively good prognosis.
items.explanation: Two steps: nephrotic proteinuria with a bland sediment means a non-proliferative lesion, and the good prognosis fits **class V membranous**.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman with newly diagnosed SLE has a malar rash, arthralgia and fatigue. Urinalysis, renal function and blood counts are normal.
questions.leadIn: Which drug should she start as the cornerstone of long-term therapy?
questions.explanation: **Hydroxychloroquine** treats skin, joint and constitutional disease, and every patient with active SLE should take it long-term to reduce flares.
whyNot: Cyclophosphamide is reserved for severe renal, CNS or cardiac disease.
Rituximab is off-label for refractory disease only.
MMF is for nephritis or disease that HCQ and low-dose steroids do not control.
Pulsed steroids are for life-threatening organ involvement.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman with SLE has stable class III lupus nephritis on mycophenolate mofetil, hydroxychloroquine and prednisolone 5 mg daily. She wants to conceive.
questions.leadIn: Which medication change is most appropriate before conception?
questions.explanation: Mycophenolate is **teratogenic** and must be stopped. **Azathioprine**, hydroxychloroquine and low-dose oral steroids are considered safe in pregnancy.
whyNot: HCQ is safe in pregnancy and stopping it risks a flare.
Low-dose prednisolone is safe in pregnancy.
Cyclophosphamide is teratogenic and causes infertility.
Continuing MMF exposes the fetus to a teratogen.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman has had SLE for 25 years. Her nephritis has been in remission for a decade on low-dose maintenance therapy.
questions.leadIn: Which is now the most likely cause of her death?
questions.explanation: Early deaths are from active renal or cerebral disease and infection. **Later**, accelerated atherosclerosis makes **coronary disease and stroke** the main causes.
whyNot: Renal deaths dominate early, and her nephritis is quiescent.
Cerebral lupus is an early cause of death.
Lymphoma risk is raised but is a much less common cause of death.
Catastrophic APS is rare and needs antiphospholipid antibodies.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman has class IV lupus nephritis and completes induction therapy. Her nephrologist reviews her response at 6 months.
questions.leadIn: Which finding best indicates a good long-term renal outlook?
options: Normalisation of proteinuria, blood pressure and renal function
Transformation to class VI on repeat biopsy
A positive ANA at high titre
A fall in CRP to normal
questions.explanation: Kumar states that treatment which **normalises proteinuria, hypertension and renal function** indicates a good prognosis.
whyNot: Anti-dsDNA may stay high even in remission and does not by itself predict renal outcome.
Class VI usually predicts ESKD.
ANA titre does not reflect activity or severity.
CRP is often normal in lupus activity and is not a renal marker.

questions.leadIn: Match each patient below with the single best option from the list. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.
options: Raise the INR target or switch to LMWH

items.stem: A 31-year-old woman with SLE has her first proximal DVT. Lupus anticoagulant has been positive on two tests 14 weeks apart.
items.explanation: APS-related VTE recurs often, so after heparin she needs **long-term warfarin**, INR 2–3 for a first venous event.

items.stem: A 29-year-old woman with APS has had three first-trimester miscarriages. She is now 6 weeks pregnant.
items.explanation: In pregnancy warfarin is contraindicated; give **LMWH plus low-dose aspirin** from early gestation.

items.stem: A 44-year-old woman with SLE and triple-positive antiphospholipid antibodies develops renal failure, a stroke and ischaemic bowel over 5 days. Biopsy shows small-vessel microthrombi.
items.explanation: Three or more organs within a week with microthrombi is **catastrophic APS**. It carries high mortality and is treated with **plasmapheresis and rituximab** as well as anticoagulation.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old man develops arthralgia and pleuritic chest pain several months after starting a new antihypertensive. ANA and anti-histone antibodies are positive.
questions.leadIn: Which drug is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: **Hydralazine** is a classic cause of drug-induced lupus, along with procainamide, isoniazid and chlorpromazine.
whyNot: Amlodipine is not among the listed culprit drugs; hydralazine is the classic antihypertensive cause.
Furosemide is linked with secondary gout, not drug-induced lupus.
Doxazosin is not among the listed culprit drugs.
Spironolactone is not among the listed culprit drugs.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man taking isoniazid for latent tuberculosis develops joint pains, a pericardial rub and a positive ANA.
questions.leadIn: Which further finding most favours drug-induced lupus over idiopathic SLE?
options: Positive anti-histone antibodies with normal complement
Red cell casts in the urine
questions.explanation: Drug-induced lupus typically gives **anti-histone positivity**, negative anti-dsDNA/anti-Sm and **normal complement**, and spares the kidney and CNS.
whyNot: Renal involvement points to idiopathic SLE.
Anti-dsDNA is usually negative in drug-induced lupus (except anti-TNF cases).
CNS involvement points to idiopathic SLE.
Anti-Sm is specific for idiopathic SLE.

questions.theme: Adverse effects of drugs used in SLE
questions.leadIn: Match each patient below with the single best option from the list. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.

items.stem: A 34-year-old woman receiving monthly IV pulses for severe lupus nephritis develops frank haematuria with clots. Urine culture is negative and platelets are normal.
items.explanation: Sterile **haemorrhagic cystitis** is caused by **cyclophosphamide** metabolites. Mesna and hydration reduce the risk.

items.stem: A 47-year-old man with SLE on a steroid-sparing agent is started on a xanthine oxidase inhibitor for gout. Three weeks later he has pancytopenia.
items.explanation: Two steps: allopurinol inhibits xanthine oxidase, which breaks down 6-mercaptopurine, so **azathioprine** levels rise and cause marrow suppression.

items.stem: A 39-year-old woman received a biologic infusion for refractory lupus-related thrombocytopenia. Months later she develops progressive weakness and confusion, and JC virus is found in the CSF.
items.explanation: **Rituximab** depletes CD20-positive B cells and rarely causes **progressive multifocal leucoencephalopathy** from JC virus.

questions.theme: Diagnosis: SLE, related conditions and mimics
questions.leadIn: Match each patient below with the single best option from the list. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.

items.stem: A 66-year-old man with heart failure has taken hydralazine for 18 months. He now has arthralgia and pleurisy. ANA and anti-histone antibodies are positive; anti-dsDNA is negative and C3/C4 are normal.
items.explanation: Classic culprit, serositis and arthritis, anti-histone positive with normal complement: **drug-induced lupus**.

items.stem: A 19-year-old woman has had white-then-blue fingers in the cold since age 14. Her mother has the same. Examination and nail-fold capillaries are normal and ANA is negative.
items.explanation: Young onset, positive family history, normal capillaries and negative ANA point to **primary Raynaud's**.

items.stem: A 34-year-old woman with known SLE has her second DVT. Anticardiolipin antibodies are positive at moderate titre on two tests 3 months apart.
items.explanation: APS with an underlying SLE diagnosis is **secondary APS**.

items.stem: A 37-year-old woman has well-defined scaly red plaques on her face and scalp, healing with scarring and patchy permanent hair loss. She has no joint, kidney or blood abnormalities.
items.explanation: Skin-only scarring plaques with no systemic features fit **chronic discoid lupus**, a benign skin-limited variant.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman has arthralgia, painless mouth ulcers and lymphopenia. ANA is positive at high titre.
questions.leadIn: Which antibody is the most specific for SLE and is associated with renal involvement?
questions.explanation: **Anti-Sm** occurs in only a minority (15–30%) but is very specific for SLE and is linked with renal disease.
whyNot: Anti-Ro also occurs in Sjögren's and is linked to photosensitivity and heart block.
Anti-La is mainly a Sjögren's marker.
Anti-RNP marks MCTD; these patients tend not to have nephritis.
Anti-histone marks drug-induced lupus.

questions.stem: A 23-year-old woman with SLE has sharp central chest pain that improves on leaning forward. A rub is heard.
questions.leadIn: Which is the most common cardiac manifestation of SLE?
questions.explanation: **Pericarditis** is the commonest cardiac feature of SLE and also counts toward the serositis criterion.
whyNot: Myocarditis occurs but is less common.
Libman–Sacks endocarditis is recognised but uncommon.
Aortic valve lesions are rare.
Heart block is a feature of neonatal lupus, not adult SLE.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman with SLE has a prolonged APTT before minor surgery. It does not correct when mixed with normal plasma. She has had one DVT.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely explanation for the prolonged APTT?
questions.explanation: An APTT prolongation that **does not correct with mixing**, in a patient with a thrombosis, is a **lupus anticoagulant**. It is prothrombotic in vivo despite the name.
whyNot: Factor deficiencies correct with mixing, and haemophilia causes bleeding, not DVT.
Vitamin K deficiency prolongs the PT and corrects with mixing.
DIC causes low platelets and fibrinogen, often with bleeding.
Factor XII deficiency corrects with mixing.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old man with diffuse proliferative lupus nephritis is about to start IV cyclophosphamide.
questions.leadIn: Which drug is given with each infusion to reduce bladder toxicity?
questions.explanation: **Mesna** binds the urotoxic metabolites of cyclophosphamide and, with good hydration, lowers the risk of haemorrhagic cystitis.
whyNot: Folinic acid is rescue for methotrexate toxicity.
Allopurinol prevents tumour lysis; it does not protect the bladder.
Ondansetron treats nausea only.
Co-trimoxazole is *Pneumocystis* prophylaxis, not bladder protection.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman with SLE presents with fever of 38.9 °C and malaise. ESR is 85 mm/h and CRP is 160 mg/L. C3 is normal and her anti-dsDNA titre is unchanged from last year. Lymphocyte count is normal.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely explanation for her presentation?
questions.explanation: Step 1: in an SLE flare the ESR rises but **CRP usually stays normal** unless there is serositis. Step 2: look at the activity markers. C3 is normal, anti-dsDNA is stable and there is no lymphopenia, so nothing suggests a flare. Step 3: a high CRP without signs of activity means **infection** until proven otherwise. Infection is also a major cause of early death in SLE.
whyNot: A flare would usually lower C3, raise anti-dsDNA and cause lymphopenia; serositis would need chest pain or a rub.
Nothing suggests a new causative drug.
Inherited deficiency would cause persistently low complement, not a high CRP.
APS presents with thrombosis or pregnancy loss, not fever with high CRP.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old woman has a fixed red rash over both cheeks sparing the nasolabial folds, and painless palatal ulcers. Platelets were 80 × 10⁹/L on two occasions a month apart. ANA is positive at high titre by immunofluorescence and anti-dsDNA is positive. Joints, urine and chest are normal.
questions.leadIn: How many of the 11 classification criteria (Davidson Box 24.63) does she meet?
questions.explanation: Go through the list. 1: **malar rash**. 2: **oral ulcers** (painless counts). 3: **haematological**, since platelets were below 100 on two occasions. 4: **immunological** (anti-dsDNA). 5: **ANA** is a separate criterion from the immunological one. That makes **5**, above the threshold of 4, so she is classified as SLE.
whyNot: Too few: this misses two of the positive criteria.
This usually comes from merging ANA and anti-dsDNA, but they are separate criteria.
Too many: arthritis, serositis, renal and neurological criteria are absent.
Too many: arthritis, serositis, renal and neurological criteria are absent.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old Black woman with SLE has haematuria, red cell casts, proteinuria of 3 g/day and creatinine rising over a month. Biopsy shows class IV diffuse proliferative lupus nephritis. She wants to have children in the future.
questions.leadIn: Which induction regimen is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: Step 1: class IV is the commonest and most severe proliferative class, so it needs **induction immunosuppression with high-dose steroids**. Step 2: the partner drug is IV cyclophosphamide or MMF, which have similar renal efficacy (Davidson). Step 3: MMF is preferred because cyclophosphamide threatens fertility and may work less well in Black and Hispanic patients. She then continues MMF for maintenance.
whyNot: HCQ benefits all classes but is not induction therapy for class IV.
An ACE inhibitor alone suits class II or mild class V, not proliferative disease.
Azathioprine is a maintenance drug and is inferior to MMF.
Rituximab is off-label rescue therapy only.

questions.theme: Choosing the right investigation in SLE
questions.leadIn: Match each patient below with the single best option from the list. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.

items.stem: A 29-year-old woman with SLE and arthritis that steroids do not control is about to start azathioprine.
items.explanation: Variants in **TPMT** affect 6-MP breakdown and the risk of marrow toxicity, so testing can guide the dose.

items.stem: A 45-year-old woman has taken hydroxychloroquine 400 mg daily for 6 years. She has no visual symptoms.
items.explanation: Hydroxychloroquine accumulates in the retina. Risk rises with long-term use and doses > 5 mg/kg/day, so **periodic retinal and visual checks** are needed.

items.stem: A 27-year-old woman with SLE has red cell casts, proteinuria of 2.4 g/day and a creatinine that has risen by 30%.
items.explanation: With active sediment, significant proteinuria and falling GFR, **renal biopsy** defines the class and guides induction treatment.

items.stem: A 50-year-old woman has needed prednisolone 10–15 mg daily for 2 years to control her SLE.
items.explanation: SLE patients, especially on long-term steroids, are at risk of osteoporosis and should be screened with **DXA**.

questions.theme: Treatment choices in SLE and related conditions
questions.leadIn: Match each patient below with the single best option from the list. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.
options: Pulsed IV methylprednisolone with IV cyclophosphamide

items.stem: A 61-year-old man on procainamide for an arrhythmia develops arthritis and a small pericardial effusion. Anti-histone antibodies are positive and complement is normal.
items.explanation: Drug-induced lupus usually resolves within 4–6 weeks of **stopping the drug**.

items.stem: A 33-year-old woman with SLE has active rash, arthritis and serositis despite hydroxychloroquine and prednisolone. Anti-dsDNA is high and C3 is low; renal and CNS function are normal.
items.explanation: Active disease that responds poorly to steroids and HCQ, especially with serological activity, is the indication for **belimumab** (anti-BLyS).

items.stem: A 26-year-old woman with SLE presents with acute psychosis and seizures. CSF shows no infection and imaging excludes other causes.
items.explanation: Severe CNS lupus is life-threatening and needs **pulsed IV methylprednisolone plus IV cyclophosphamide** (Davidson regimen).

items.stem: A 35-year-old woman with newly diagnosed SLE takes no regular medication. She has microscopic haematuria and low-level proteinuria with normal blood pressure and renal function. Biopsy shows mesangial hypercellularity only.
items.explanation: Two steps: mesangial-only change is **class II**, which needs no intensive immunosuppression (an ACE inhibitor is an optional add-on). **Hydroxychloroquine** benefits all classes and is her baseline drug.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old woman with SLE has taken hydroxychloroquine for 10 years. She weighs 50 kg and takes 400 mg daily.
questions.leadIn: Which complication of her treatment is the main reason for regular monitoring?
questions.explanation: She takes 8 mg/kg/day, above the 5 mg/kg threshold that raises the risk of **retinal toxicity** (up to 7.5% with long-term use). Visual checks are needed before and during treatment.
whyNot: Haemorrhagic cystitis is caused by cyclophosphamide.
Hypogammaglobulinaemia follows rituximab.
Not a recognised effect of hydroxychloroquine.
Not a recognised effect of hydroxychloroquine.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man with SLE takes azathioprine 150 mg daily. He develops tophaceous gout and allopurinol is to be started.
questions.leadIn: What change to his azathioprine is required?
options: Give it on alternate days at the same dose
questions.explanation: Allopurinol blocks the breakdown of azathioprine/6-MP, so the azathioprine dose must be cut by about **75%** to avoid marrow suppression.
whyNot: Increasing the dose would worsen toxicity.
Without a reduction, levels rise and marrow suppression follows.
Cyclophosphamide is for severe organ-threatening disease, not a drug interaction.
Alternate-day dosing is only about a 50% reduction and is not the recommended adjustment.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman with SLE is started on a monoclonal antibody infusion after poor response to steroids and hydroxychloroquine. It blocks a cytokine that B cells need to survive.
questions.leadIn: What is the target of this drug?
questions.explanation: **Belimumab** binds **BAFF (BLyS)**, which B cells need to survive and function. It is used after an inadequate response to steroids and HCQ.
whyNot: CD20 is the target of rituximab, which lyses B cells directly.
Anti-TNF drugs are used in RA and spondyloarthritis and can cause drug-induced lupus.
IL-6 receptor is the target of tocilizumab.
IMPDH is inhibited by mycophenolate, an oral drug.

questions.theme: Interpreting abnormal results in a patient with SLE
questions.leadIn: Match each patient below with the single best option from the list. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.

items.stem: A 36-year-old woman with SLE has had low C3 and C4 at every visit for 8 years, even when clinically well with normal anti-dsDNA. Her sister has a similar complement profile.
items.explanation: Persistently low C3/C4 regardless of activity, with an affected relative, points to **inherited complement deficiency** rather than consumption.

items.stem: A 28-year-old woman started prednisolone 40 mg daily for lupus pleurisy one week ago. She feels better and her chest pain has gone. White cell count is 14 × 10⁹/L (neutrophils 12) with no fever and a normal CRP.
items.explanation: Two steps: she is improving, afebrile, with normal CRP, so neither infection nor a flare explains it. Steroids raise the **neutrophil count**: this is a **glucocorticoid effect**.

items.stem: A 27-year-old woman with SLE has a falling haemoglobin, raised bilirubin and reticulocytes, and a positive direct Coombs test.
items.explanation: Coombs-positive haemolysis is antibody-mediated destruction: **autoimmune haemolytic anaemia**, a haematological criterion.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman is referred after pregnancy losses. Lupus anticoagulant was positive 14 weeks ago and is positive again today.
questions.leadIn: Which obstetric history would satisfy the clinical criteria for antiphospholipid syndrome?
options: Three consecutive unexplained miscarriages before 10 weeks
A single preterm birth at 37 weeks
questions.explanation: APS obstetric criteria include **≥ 3 recurrent first-trimester (< 10 week) miscarriages**, an unexplained fetal death after 10 weeks, or severe early pre-eclampsia/premature birth before 34 weeks.
whyNot: A single early miscarriage is common and not enough.
Hyperemesis is not an APS criterion.
Gestational diabetes is not an APS criterion.
Birth at 37 weeks is term; the criterion is premature birth before 34 weeks.

questions.theme: Neurological and psychiatric presentations in SLE
questions.leadIn: Match each patient below with the single best option from the list. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.

items.stem: A 25-year-old woman started prednisolone 60 mg daily 5 days ago for a lupus flare. She now sleeps 2 hours a night, talks rapidly and feels elated. Her flare is settling and complement is improving.
items.explanation: Two steps: the flare is improving, which argues against cerebral lupus. Rapid steroid changes can cause **mania and insomnia**, a glucocorticoid mood disturbance.

items.stem: A 34-year-old woman with SLE and triple-positive antiphospholipid antibodies has sudden right arm and face weakness with dysphasia.
items.explanation: Antiphospholipid antibodies cause arterial thrombosis; **ischaemic stroke** affects about 20% of APS patients.

items.stem: A 29-year-old woman with active SLE develops weakness of both legs over 2 days, a sensory level at T8 and urinary retention. MRI of the brain is normal.
items.explanation: Bilateral leg weakness with a **sensory level** and sphincter involvement is **transverse myelitis**, a specific feature of CNS lupus (also linked with APS).

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman asks about her long-term outlook after a new diagnosis of SLE with mild skin and joint disease.
questions.leadIn: Which statement about prognosis in SLE is correct?
options: Ten-year survival is about 90%, lower with major organ involvement
Mortality is no different from the general population
Men have milder disease than women
Childhood-onset disease is milder than adult-onset disease
questions.explanation: Kumar gives a 10-year survival of about **90%**, reduced by major organ disease. Davidson reports a fivefold mortality increase, mainly from premature cardiovascular disease.
whyNot: Lymphoma risk is raised, but cardiovascular disease, renal/CNS disease and infection cause more deaths.
Mortality is about five times that of matched controls.
Men have more severe disease.
Childhood-onset disease is more severe, with more renal involvement.

ospe.identify: Malar (butterfly) rash of SLE: fixed erythema over the cheeks **sparing the nasolabial folds**. Differential: rosacea.
Severe secondary Raynaud's phenomenon with **digital ulceration**, suggesting an autoimmune connective tissue disease such as SLE.
Chronic **discoid lupus**: scaly plaques that heal with atrophy and hypopigmentation, unlike the macular malar erythema of SLE.
Butterfly rash across the cheeks and nasal bridge: SLE spot diagnosis. Next step: ANA, then specific antibodies.
**Livedo reticularis**: net-like violaceous mottling seen in SLE and **antiphospholipid syndrome**. Ask about thrombosis and pregnancy loss.
Renal biopsy: **class IV diffuse proliferative lupus nephritis**, with endothelial and mesangial proliferation across glomeruli.
